variants.title: Construct the dataset
variants.context: Dataset construction runs in four stages: define a narrow capability, author contexts and choices, filter artifacts and ambiguity, then freeze an independent split. Each stage decides which shortcuts a model can exploit and which conclusions stay defensible.
variants.prompt: A team is building a new two-choice benchmark for physical affordances in the style of PIQA. Put the construction stages in order, ending with the split that tuning has not consumed.

items.text: Freeze a versioned, independent split with protected items and reproducible scoring.
Define the narrow capability: choosing which of two methods physically achieves an everyday goal.
Filter easy lexical cues and disputed gold labels with adversarial filtering and independent review.
Author a goal, one intended solution, and a plausible distractor for each item under a documented procedure.

variants.hint: Filtering can only remove cues from items that already exist.
variants.explanation: Claim, items, quality, then evidence: the capability is defined first and the split is frozen last so the comparison is not consumed by tuning.

variants.title: Construct the dataset
variants.context: Dataset construction runs in four stages: define a narrow capability, author contexts and choices, filter artifacts and ambiguity, then freeze an independent split. Each stage decides which shortcuts a model can exploit and which conclusions stay defensible.
variants.prompt: A team wants a Winograd-style set at WinoGrande scale, about 44,000 problems, with AfLite reducing embedding-detectable associations. Put the stages in order and place AfLite where it belongs.

items.text: Run AfLite to remove problems that embeddings can solve through incidental associations.
Have authors write sentence pairs where changing the context flips the correct referent.
Freeze the training-size variants and the evaluation split so published variants are never mixed silently.
Define the capability: resolve a blank to one of two entities when syntax alone is insufficient.

variants.hint: AfLite is a quality filter, so it needs authored items to filter.
variants.explanation: AfLite belongs in the filtering stage, after items exist and before the split is frozen, and the frozen variants must be named so different training sizes are not compared as one.

variants.title: Construct the dataset
variants.context: Dataset construction runs in four stages: define a narrow capability, author contexts and choices, filter artifacts and ambiguity, then freeze an independent split. Each stage decides which shortcuts a model can exploit and which conclusions stay defensible.
variants.prompt: A team is authoring SocialIQA-style three-choice questions about intent and reaction. Independent reviewers found that the first batch had stylistic cues in the distractors. Put the full construction in order, including the review that found the problem.

items.text: Collect a context, one intended answer, and two distractors per item under a documented collection procedure.
Define the capability: inferring a person's likely intent, reaction, need, or emotion from a short social situation.
Review the batch independently and remove distractors that carry simple stylistic cues.
Freeze a versioned split kept independent from prompt development, and report the sampling rule.

variants.hint: The review that found the cue is the quality stage, not the authoring stage.
variants.explanation: Distractor review is part of filtering artifacts and ambiguity; it happens after authoring and before the split is frozen as evidence.

variants.title: Turn a failure into evidence
variants.context: A wrong multiple-choice answer becomes useful only after it changes the evaluation or the system. The path runs from a frozen benchmark run, to a failure review that names the cause, to a product challenge that recreates the failure, to a bounded release gate.
variants.prompt: A story-continuation product fails several HellaSwag items in its frozen run. Put the steps in order that turn those failures into a release decision.

items.text: Review each failure and separate missing knowledge, invalid inference, ambiguity, extraction error, and shortcut behavior.
Run the benchmark under the frozen protocol and record raw outputs and per-slice results.
Recreate the failure with the product prompt, tools, language, and user consequences.
Gate the release on critical slices, robustness checks, and a monitored canary before widening exposure.

variants.hint: You cannot recreate a failure in the product until you know what kind of failure it is.
variants.explanation: Run, review the cause, challenge with the product, then gate: each stage feeds the next, and the gate stays bounded.

variants.title: Turn a failure into evidence
variants.context: A wrong multiple-choice answer becomes useful only after it changes the evaluation or the system. The path runs from a frozen benchmark run, to a failure review that names the cause, to a product challenge that recreates the failure, to a bounded release gate.
variants.prompt: A meeting-notes summarizer resolves a pronoun to the wrong person on WinoGrande items. The team suspects extraction, not inference. Put the steps in order, including the cause decision.

items.text: Compare raw responses with extracted labels to decide whether the errors are extraction errors or invalid inference.
Require the referent slice to clear its floor and a monitored canary before widening exposure.
Rebuild the surviving inference failures as product prompts with real meeting transcripts.
Record the raw responses and extracted labels from the frozen WinoGrande run.

variants.hint: Cause, not label: decide what kind of failure it is before spending product effort on it.
variants.explanation: Failure review separates extraction errors from inference errors first, so the product challenge only recreates the failures that are real.

variants.title: Turn a failure into evidence
variants.context: A wrong multiple-choice answer becomes useful only after it changes the evaluation or the system. The path runs from a frozen benchmark run, to a failure review that names the cause, to a product challenge that recreates the failure, to a bounded release gate.
variants.prompt: After launch, real users report the product choosing an impossible tool for a task. Put the operating cadence in order, from the launch-time sample to the protected set that future releases will use.

items.text: Keep that protected set out of tuning so it stays independent evidence.
Measure the sampled failures by product slice.
Recreate the representative cases with the product prompt and user consequences.
Sample real failures from production traffic after launch.
Promote validated cases into a future protected set.

variants.hint: Measurement comes before promotion; a case earns protected status only after it is validated.
variants.explanation: The after-launch cadence samples, measures, validates, and then promotes cases into a protected set that must not leak into tuning.

variants.title: Compute the chance baseline
variants.context: Expected chance-correct items depend on the number of answer options: two-choice PIQA and WinoGrande sit at 50 percent, three-choice SocialIQA at 33.3 percent, four-choice HellaSwag and OpenBookQA at 25 percent, and five-choice CommonsenseQA at 20 percent. Raw accuracy should never be compared without that baseline.
variants.prompt: A portfolio samples 240 HellaSwag items. How many items would uniform random guessing be expected to get right?
variants.hint: How many options does a HellaSwag item have?
variants.explanation: HellaSwag has four options, so chance is 25 percent and 240 x 0.25 = 60 expected chance-correct items.

mistakes.feedback: That assumes two options; HellaSwag has four continuations per item.
That assumes five options; five-choice is CommonsenseQA, not HellaSwag.

variants.title: Compute the chance baseline
variants.context: Expected chance-correct items depend on the number of answer options: two-choice PIQA and WinoGrande sit at 50 percent, three-choice SocialIQA at 33.3 percent, four-choice HellaSwag and OpenBookQA at 25 percent, and five-choice CommonsenseQA at 20 percent. Raw accuracy should never be compared without that baseline.
variants.prompt: A model scores 62 percent on a 500-item CommonsenseQA sample. How many percentage points above the chance baseline is that?
variants.hint: Chance is one over the number of choices, and CommonsenseQA is five-choice.
variants.explanation: CommonsenseQA has five choices, so chance is 20 percent and 62 minus 20 = 42 points above chance.

mistakes.feedback: That subtracts a 25 percent four-choice baseline; CommonsenseQA has five choices.
That subtracts a 50 percent binary baseline, which belongs to PIQA or WinoGrande.

variants.title: Compute the chance baseline
variants.context: Expected chance-correct items depend on the number of answer options: two-choice PIQA and WinoGrande sit at 50 percent, three-choice SocialIQA at 33.3 percent, four-choice HellaSwag and OpenBookQA at 25 percent, and five-choice CommonsenseQA at 20 percent. Raw accuracy should never be compared without that baseline.
variants.prompt: A portfolio samples 120 PIQA items, 120 SocialIQA items, and 160 CommonsenseQA items. How many items in total would random guessing be expected to get right?
variants.hint: Compute each benchmark separately using its own option count, then add.
variants.explanation: 120 x 0.5 = 60, 120 x 0.333 = 40, and 160 x 0.2 = 32, which sums to 132 chance-correct items.

mistakes.feedback: That applies one four-option baseline to all 400 items; each benchmark has its own option count.
That treats every item as two-choice; only PIQA is binary here.

variants.title: Keep the comparison honest
variants.context: A score is comparable only under its four labels: dataset and split, prompt and decoding contract, baseline, and scope. Replacing the frozen comparison prompt with a product prompt makes a run diagnostic rather than comparable, and product weights count only when they were declared before the candidate result was seen.
variants.prompt: A team reruns PIQA with its own product system prompt instead of the frozen comparison prompt and reports the result next to a public leaderboard number. What is the correct status of that run?
options: Invalid, because a product prompt can never be used in a benchmark.
Diagnostic: relevant to the product but no longer directly comparable to the public result.
Comparable, because the dataset and split are unchanged.
optionFeedback: Product prompts are useful; they just need to be labeled as diagnostic rather than comparable.
The prompt contract changed, so the run informs the product without being a like-for-like comparison.
Dataset identity is one label of four; the prompt and decoding contract also has to match.
variants.hint: Which of the four labels changed, and what does that change do to comparability?
variants.explanation: Protocol status becomes diagnostic when a product prompt replaces the frozen comparison prompt; the run is relevant but not directly comparable.

variants.title: Keep the comparison honest
variants.context: A score is comparable only under its four labels: dataset and split, prompt and decoding contract, baseline, and scope. Replacing the frozen comparison prompt with a product prompt makes a run diagnostic rather than comparable, and product weights count only when they were declared before the candidate result was seen.
variants.prompt: A team reports 78 percent on WinoGrande and compares it with a paper's number, but the paper used a different published training-size variant. What should the team do?
options: Report both numbers as directly comparable, since the task is the same.
Name the exact variant and split in the report and refuse to present the two numbers as one comparison.
Drop the paper's number and report only the team's score without a baseline.
optionFeedback: WinoGrande's training-size variants must not be mixed silently; the task name is not enough.
The dataset and split label must name the variant, so the mismatch stays visible.
Every score needs a baseline; the fix is a matching one, not none.
variants.hint: The first of the four labels is dataset and split, and it includes the version.
variants.explanation: Different published WinoGrande variants must not be mixed silently; the dataset label names the exact variant so the comparison is honest.

variants.title: Keep the comparison honest
variants.context: A score is comparable only under its four labels: dataset and split, prompt and decoding contract, baseline, and scope. Replacing the frozen comparison prompt with a product prompt makes a run diagnostic rather than comparable, and product weights count only when they were declared before the candidate result was seen.
variants.prompt: After seeing that a candidate is weak on SocialIQA, a product manager proposes lowering SocialIQA's weight in the portfolio aggregate. What is the defensible response?
options: Keep the declared weights for this candidate and show per-benchmark scores beside the aggregate.
Accept the new weights, because product priorities are the manager's call.
Switch to a macro average so no weights are needed anywhere.
optionFeedback: Product weights count only when declared before the result, and per-benchmark scores must stay visible.
Weights chosen after seeing the candidate result turn the aggregate into a tuned number.
A macro average is a valid choice, but changing the aggregation after seeing the result has the same problem.
variants.hint: When were the weights declared relative to the result?
variants.explanation: Use product weights only when they were declared before seeing the candidate result, and always show the per-benchmark scores beside the aggregate.

variants.title: Name the failure cause
variants.context: Failure review separates causes rather than labels: missing knowledge, invalid inference, ambiguity, extraction error, and shortcut behavior. Each cause points at a different repair, from a better extractor to a counterfactual challenge set.
variants.prompt: On OpenBookQA the model answers 'The answer is B, though C is also defensible.' The harness records the item as invalid and counts it wrong. Which cause is this?
options: Missing knowledge: the model lacked the core science fact.
Extraction error: the answer-extraction rule could not map a valid response to one label.
Invalid inference: the model reasoned to the wrong conclusion.
optionFeedback: Nothing here shows a knowledge gap; the record failed at extraction.
The response contains a label; the extractor, not the model's reasoning, dropped it.
The model chose B; whether B is right is a separate question from why it was scored invalid.
variants.hint: Compare the raw response with the extracted label before judging the reasoning.
variants.explanation: When the raw response holds a usable answer but the harness records invalid, the cause is an extraction error and the fix is in the extractor.

variants.title: Name the failure cause
variants.context: Failure review separates causes rather than labels: missing knowledge, invalid inference, ambiguity, extraction error, and shortcut behavior. Each cause points at a different repair, from a better extractor to a counterfactual challenge set.
variants.prompt: A model's HellaSwag accuracy drops 18 points when every option is padded to the same length while the answer logic is untouched. Which cause does this reveal?
options: Shortcut behavior: the model was using answer length instead of the intended relation.
Missing knowledge: the model does not know the events described.
Ambiguity: the padded items no longer have a clear gold label.
optionFeedback: A meaning-preserving cue removal that flips answers isolates dependence on that cue.
Knowledge did not change between the original and the counterfactual; only the cue did.
The perturbation kept the answer logic fixed, so the gold labels are unchanged.
variants.hint: What changed between the paired items, and what stayed the same?
variants.explanation: A counterfactual that removes one incidental cue while preserving the answer exposes shortcut behavior, not a knowledge or ambiguity problem.

variants.title: Name the failure cause
variants.context: Failure review separates causes rather than labels: missing knowledge, invalid inference, ambiguity, extraction error, and shortcut behavior. Each cause points at a different repair, from a better extractor to a counterfactual challenge set.
variants.prompt: Two independent reviewers disagree about the gold label on a CommonsenseQA item the model got wrong. Which cause should the review assign, and what follows?
options: Ambiguity; remove the disputed item from the protected evidence.
Invalid inference; keep the item and count the miss against the model.
Shortcut behavior; add the item to the counterfactual set.
optionFeedback: Disputed gold labels are ambiguity, and the repair is to remove ambiguous items.
A disputed gold label cannot support a verdict about the model's inference.
Nothing shows the model relied on an incidental cue here.
variants.hint: Can a miss count against the model when humans do not agree on the answer?
variants.explanation: Ambiguity is a dataset failure, not a model failure; repair the evidence by removing disputed items rather than scoring them.
